items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider the function [MATH: f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}] defined by [MATH: f(x)=3x+2.] Let's prove that this function is injective.

Content:
First, we recall the definition of an injection:

Content:
> A function [MATH: f: X\rightarrow Y] is an injection if every element [MATH: x\in X] is mapped to a distinct element in [MATH: Y{:}]
> [MATH: x_1 \neq x_2
> \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
> f(x_1) \neq f(x_2)]

Content:
This statement contains some negations. Thus, it's easier to show that a function is injective using the (equivalent) contrapositive statement:

Content:
> This implication is equivalent to its contrapositive:
> [MATH: f(x_1)=f(x_2)
> \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
> x_1=x_2]

Content:
Therefore, the injectivity of [MATH: f] means the following:

Content:
> In our case, for all [MATH: x_1,x_2 \in \mathbb{R},]
> [MATH: 3x_1+2
> =
> 3x_2+2
> \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
> x_1
> =
> x_2.]

Content:
So, to prove the injectivity of [MATH: f,] we need to derive [MATH: x_1=x_2] by assuming that [MATH: f(x_1)=f(x_2){:}]

Content:
We begin our proof as follows:

Content:
> Let [MATH: x_1,x_2 \in \mathbb{R},] and suppose that [MATH: f(x_1)=f(x_2).] Then, we have the following:
> [MATH: f(x_{1})|= f(x_{2}); 3x_{1} + 2|= 3x_{2} + 2; 3x_{1}|= 3x_{2}; x_{1}|= x_{2}]

Content:
This proves that [MATH: f(x_1) = f(x_2)] implies [MATH: x_1 = x_2.]

Content:
Finally, we state the conclusion:

Content:
> Hence, [MATH: x_1=x_2,] as was to be shown. Therefore, [MATH: f] is an injection.

Content:
For clarity, let's restate our proposition and its proof.

sections.normalized_html: What does it mean for the function [MATH: f: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{N}] defined by [MATH: f(x)=3x^2+1] to be NOT injective?
sections.readable_text: What does it mean for the function [MATH: f: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{N}] defined by [MATH: f(x)=3x^2+1] to be NOT injective?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
A function [MATH: f: X\rightarrow Y] is an injection if every element [MATH: x\in X] is mapped to a distinct element in [MATH: Y.]

In other words, [MATH: \forall x_1, x_2 \: \big( x_1 \neq x_2 \Rightarrow f(x_1) \neq f(x_2) \big).] The negation of this statement is [MATH: \exists x_1, x_2 \: \lnot \big( x_1 \neq x_2 \Rightarrow f(x_1) \neq f(x_2) \big).] Now, recall that [MATH: ¬(A⇒B)|≡¬(¬A∨B); ≡¬(¬A)∧¬B; ≡A∧¬B]

So, to determine non-injectivity, we need to show that there exists [MATH: x_1,x_2] such that [MATH: x_1 \neq x_2 \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad f(x_1) = f(x_2).]

In our case, the non-injectivity of [MATH: f] means that [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{there exist}}] at least two values [MATH: x_1] and [MATH: x_2] such that [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}x_1 \neq x_2} \qquad \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{and}} \qquad \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}3x_1^2+1 = 3x_2^2+1}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:

A function [MATH: f: X\rightarrow Y] is an injection if every element [MATH: x\in X] is mapped to a distinct element in [MATH: Y{:}] [MATH: x_1 \neq x_2 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad f(x_1) \neq f(x_2)]

In this case, it would be easier to prove the contrapositive statement.

This implication is equivalent to its contrapositive: [MATH: f(x_1)=f(x_2) \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad x_1=x_2]

Now, we simply need to derive [MATH: z_1=z_2] by assuming that [MATH: f(z_1)=f(z_2){:}]

So, let [MATH: z_1,z_2 \in \mathbb{C},] and suppose that [MATH: f(z_1)=f(z_2).] Then, we have [MATH: f(z_{1})|= f(z_{2}); ((1)/(2)(z_{1} + z_{1}^(―)), (\textrm{i})/(2)(z_{1}^(―) − z_{1}))|= ((1)/(2)(z_{2} + z_{2}^(―)), (\textrm{i})/(2)(z_{2}^(―) − z_{2})).] Since two pairs are equal if and only if their respective components are equal, we obtain: [MATH: {(1)/(2)(z_{1} + z_{1}^(―)) = (1)/(2)(z_{2} + z_{2}^(―)); (\textrm{i})/(2)(z_{1}^(―) − z_{1}) = (\textrm{i})/(2)(z_{2}^(―) − z_{2})|⇒{z_{1} + z_{1}^(―) = z_{2} + z_{2}^(―); z_{1}^(―) − z_{1} = z_{2}^(―) − z_{2}] To solve this system, recall the following properties of the complex conjugate: [MATH: z_1+\overline{z_1} = 2\cdot \textrm{Re}(z_1), \qquad z_1-\overline{z_1} = 2\textrm{i}\cdot \textrm{Im}(z_1)] Therefore, our system reduces to [MATH: {2 ⋅ Re(z_{1}) = 2 ⋅ Re(z_{2}); − 2\textrm{i} ⋅ Im(z_{1}) = − 2\textrm{i} ⋅ Im(z_{2})|⇒{Re(z_{1}) = Re(z_{2}); Im(z_{1}) = Im(z_{2})|⇒z_{1} = z_{2}]

Finally, we state the conclusion:

Hence, [MATH: z_1=z_2,] as was to be shown. Therefore, [MATH: f] is an injection.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the function [MATH: f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}] defined by [MATH: f(x)=3x+2.] Let's prove that this function is injective.

Content:
First, we recall the definition of an injection:

Content:
> A function [MATH: f: X\rightarrow Y] is an injection if every element [MATH: x\in X] is mapped to a distinct element in [MATH: Y{:}]
> [MATH: x_1 \neq x_2
> \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
> f(x_1) \neq f(x_2)]

Content:
This statement contains some negations. Thus, it's easier to show that a function is injective using the (equivalent) contrapositive statement:

Content:
> This implication is equivalent to its contrapositive:
> [MATH: f(x_1)=f(x_2)
> \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
> x_1=x_2]

Content:
Therefore, the injectivity of [MATH: f] means the following:

Content:
> In our case, for all [MATH: x_1,x_2 \in \mathbb{R},]
> [MATH: 3x_1+2
> =
> 3x_2+2
> \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
> x_1
> =
> x_2.]

Content:
So, to prove the injectivity of [MATH: f,] we need to derive [MATH: x_1=x_2] by assuming that [MATH: f(x_1)=f(x_2){:}]

Content:
We begin our proof as follows:

Content:
> Let [MATH: x_1,x_2 \in \mathbb{R},] and suppose that [MATH: f(x_1)=f(x_2).] Then, we have the following:
> [MATH: f(x_{1})|= f(x_{2}); 3x_{1} + 2|= 3x_{2} + 2; 3x_{1}|= 3x_{2}; x_{1}|= x_{2}]

Content:
This proves that [MATH: f(x_1) = f(x_2)] implies [MATH: x_1 = x_2.]

Content:
Finally, we state the conclusion:

Content:
> Hence, [MATH: x_1=x_2,] as was to be shown. Therefore, [MATH: f] is an injection.
